The July 28, 2021 FOMC statement is broadly supportive and deliberately dovish: policy rates held at 0–0.25%, ongoing QE of $80B Treasuries and $40B agency MBS, and explicit tolerance for inflation “moderately above 2 percent for some time.” Within the Clarida‑Galí‑Gertler framework on monetary policy rules and expectations, this combination of forward guidance and a make-up strategy (average inflation targeting, as announced by Chair Powell at Jackson Hole 2020) aims to anchor longer-term inflation expectations near 2% while lowering real rates today—conditions typically associated with easier financial conditions and a constructive near-term macro outlook. 

Implementation details (e.g., setting the interest on reserve balances at 0.15% and operating via ample-reserves tools) align with Goodfriend’s analysis of modern operating frameworks, supporting precise control of the funds rate at the zero lower bound. Consistent with the Taylor-rule literature, the choice to keep rates low despite rising inflation reflects a systematic, state-contingent deviation justified by AIT—acting as insurance against ZLB scarring while supply and pandemic shocks abate—rather than a loss of discipline. Forward guidance and QE, documented in Fed practice and the term-structure literature (e.g., Cochrane–Piazzesi’s focus on risk premia), are likely to compress term premiums and keep financial conditions accommodative, which the statement notes. 

Balancing these positive supports are explicit downside risks (“path of the economy continues to depend on the course of the virus”) and the acknowledgement that pandemic-impacted sectors had “not fully recovered.” On net—strong policy support, credible framework-based guidance, and improving activity offsetting lingering health and supply risks—the tone skews moderately positive.
